tagline: Farm valleys, mountain overlooks and a camp’s remains in northwest Georgia
intro: The Ridge and Valley Scenic Byway travels 51 miles through northwest Georgia on US 27, State Highways 156 and 136, and rural county roads. Georgia DOT includes it among the state’s designated scenic byways, highlighting mountain overlooks, farmland and surviving nineteenth-century farmhouses. A steep gravel spur climbs to the deck at John’s Mountain Overlook. At The Pocket, Horn Mountain curves beside a basin bounded on the west by Mill Mountain and Johns Mountain.

At The Pocket, a Civilian Conservation Corps camp established in 1938 preceded the recreation area. The camp buildings were demolished after it closed, but a springhouse foundation and a large shower-house floor survive. The Forest Service confirms that camp remnants remain visible near the picnic shelter.

From Subligna, the journey heads toward Villanow. John’s Mountain Overlook is an excursion off the byway, reached by its own steep gravel approach. The route then takes in The Pocket and Everett Springs before Armuchee on US 27, nine miles north of Rome.

moments.title: Subligna
moments.text: The name honors Dr. William Dunlap Underwood with a construction meaning “under wood.” A post office operated here from 1848 to 1953. Georgia incorporated the town in 1870, then repealed its municipal charter in 1995. The community remains unincorporated in Chattooga County.

moments.title: Villanow
moments.text: Cavender’s Store in Villanow has walls eighteen inches thick, built of handmade brick on a rock foundation. The store supplied goods ranging from buggies to caskets. Cavender also operated a buggy and wagon shop, a blacksmith shop and a cotton mill on the property. The building entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1992. It no longer operates as a country store; the building has become a chiropractic office and private residence. Its one-story form has a front-facing gable, brickwork laid in American bond, and iron rods tying the structure together.

moments.title: John's Mountain Overlook
moments.text: A steep gravel road leads off the byway to John’s Mountain Overlook, ending at a small gravel parking area and an observation deck. The site also has a 3.5-mile hiking loop. The approach is seasonal: the road closes during the winter, from January through early March.

moments.title: The Pocket
moments.text: The Pocket takes its name from the curve of Horn Mountain, which encloses this basin in northern Floyd County. Horn Mountain bounds the valley to the south and east; Mill Mountain and Johns Mountain stand to the west. A Civilian Conservation Corps camp began here in 1938. After it closed, its buildings were demolished. The surviving springhouse foundation and shower-house floor preserve traces of the camp within a place now equipped with a campground, picnic area and trails. The valley also formerly held a watermill, cotton gin and a sawmill.
moments.notice: Camp remnants remain visible in the picnic-shelter area.

practical: John's Mountain Overlook: The steep gravel access road closes January through early March. (checked 2026-10-11)
